Kristian Andersen, PhD: The Andersen lab studies the relationship between disease-causing pathogens and their hosts, trying to understand how dangerous viruses emerge, spread, and evolve. The lab has worked on SARS-CoV-2, Zika, Ebola, West Nile, and Lassa viruses, combining next-generation genome sequencing, fieldwork in outbreak regions, laboratory experiments, and computational biology. Much of the work is done through large international collaborations, since tracking an outbreak in real time requires many labs and countries working together. A notable example of this approach was tracing the early spread of COVID-19 back to a market in Wuhan by analyzing genetic samples. This kind of research helps scientists and public health officials detect new outbreaks earlier and respond faster, which matters because catching a dangerous pathogen's spread early can prevent it from becoming a global pandemic.
Ahmed Badran, PhD: The Badran lab works on engineering biomolecules, including some of the central molecular machines found in living cells, with the goal of developing new medicines and new ways to fight climate change. One major project is re-engineering RuBisCO, the enzyme plants use to capture carbon dioxide during photosynthesis, to make it better at pulling CO2 out of the atmosphere. This ties into broader interest in synthetic biology strategies inspired by how plants and other organisms naturally manage chemistry. The lab has also worked on methods for building new-to-nature proteins using expanded genetic codes. This research matters because it could lead to both new therapeutic approaches and biotechnology tools for addressing rising atmospheric carbon dioxide and its environmental effects on agriculture and climate.
William Balch, PhD: The Balch lab studies how genetic variation across human populations affects the way proteins fold, and how misfolding contributes to disease and aging. They combine cell biology, biochemistry, and structural biology experiments with computational and machine-learning tools (including Gaussian Process models) to analyze, at the level of individual amino acids, how a protein's shape and function change in response to genetic mutations and cellular stress. A key focus is the proteostasis machinery, the cellular systems (like Hsp70 and Hsp90 chaperones) that help proteins fold correctly. The lab has shown that some genetic diseases can potentially be treated not by fixing the mutated gene, but by helping the resulting protein fold properly. This approach aims to build a general framework for understanding and correcting protein-folding problems across many different genetic diseases.
Phil Baran, PhD: The Baran lab is an organic chemistry lab focused on finding the most efficient, practical ways to build complex, biologically important molecules from scratch, a goal they call the 'ideal synthesis.' They pioneered techniques based on radical chemistry that complement traditional chemical bond-forming methods, dramatically cutting the number of steps needed to make complex natural products (for example, reducing one synthesis from 40-55 steps down to 19). The lab has invented widely used tools such as sulfinate salts, redox-active esters for coupling reactions, and methods for building therapeutic oligonucleotides, and it helped popularize modern electrochemistry in organic synthesis through the ElectraSyn device. These innovations are applied to make drugs, agrochemicals, and other materials faster, cheaper, and more sustainably, accelerating drug discovery and reducing waste in chemical manufacturing.
Donna Blackmond, PhD: The Blackmond lab develops and applies a method called Reaction Progress Kinetic Analysis (RPKA), which uses precise real-time measurements of a chemical reaction as it happens, combined with mathematical analysis, to figure out how reactions work and to propose mechanisms rather than just confirm ones already suspected. This approach has been applied to understand complex catalytic reactions used in the pharmaceutical industry, including asymmetric hydrogenation and metal-catalyzed bond-forming reactions, helping streamline how new drugs are manufactured. The lab has also studied 'nonlinear effects' in catalysis and used these ideas to investigate one of chemistry's deepest questions: why biological molecules like amino acids in living things overwhelmingly favor one mirror-image form over another (homochirality), including how enantiomer-enriched mixtures could arise from nearly equal starting mixtures.
Michael Boddy, PhD: The Boddy lab studies the molecular machinery cells use to detect and repair DNA damage, which is essential because errors in DNA copying or damage from environmental stress can lead to genome instability that drives cancer and premature aging. They also study how some of these same DNA-repair proteins have a second job in the innate immune response, helping cells detect and respond to circular DNA molecules such as viruses and gene therapy vectors. Using cell biology, proteomics, genetics, and structural biology, the lab discovered a novel protein family called STUbLs (SUMO-targeted ubiquitin ligases), revealing new crosstalk between two major protein-modification systems in cells and explaining how a leukemia drug works. This work connects basic DNA repair biology to cancer, aging, and antiviral defense.
Dale L. Boger, PhD: The Boger lab develops new strategies and methods for synthesizing complex molecules, with applications spanning antibiotics, chronic pain treatment, and cancer therapy. Their work includes redesigning the antibiotic vancomycin to create more durable, effective versions capable of overcoming bacterial resistance, as well as achieving the total synthesis of complex natural products like vinblastine. The lab has also explored specialized chemical reactions, such as inverse electron demand Diels-Alder reactions, to build difficult molecular structures. This research matters because bacteria are increasingly resistant to existing antibiotics and the pipeline of new ones has slowed, while the group's broader synthesis methods also open doors to new pharmaceuticals and chemical probes for studying and treating disease.
Michael Bollong, PhD: The Bollong lab works on regenerative medicine, which means finding ways to help the body repair its own damaged tissues and organs rather than just managing disease symptoms. They combine traditional drug discovery approaches with modern biological techniques to identify the molecular pathways that control tissue regeneration, then develop small-molecule medicines that can activate those pathways. Their work targets a range of conditions including heart disease, inflammatory disease, and fibrosis. One product of this research, developed through Scripps Research's drug discovery arm Calibr-Skaggs, is an inhaled drug called CMR316 designed to stimulate lung stem cells and regenerate damaged lung tissue in diseases like idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; it is currently being tested in a phase 1 clinical trial for safety.
Bryan Briney, PhD: The Briney lab studies antibodies and the immune system's response to dangerous viruses, with the goal of guiding vaccine design. Their work spans HIV, Lassa virus, SARS-related coronaviruses, and other pathogens, using approaches like comparing antibody and viral protein structures across virus lineages and high-throughput sequencing of antibody repertoires to identify rare, especially effective antibodies. This research has helped identify new antibodies and vaccine targets for Lassa virus, uncovered antibodies that broadly protect against SARS viruses including emerging variants, and contributed to efforts toward an HIV vaccine. The lab collaborates with organizations like IAVI and works across multiple viral disease areas, aiming to develop vaccines and therapeutic antibodies that could be stockpiled ahead of future pandemics.
Dennis Burton, PhD: The Burton lab is a leader in the study of broadly neutralizing antibodies, the rare antibodies capable of fighting off many different strains of a highly variable virus. Their research focuses primarily on HIV and, more recently, coronaviruses, working to isolate and characterize these antibodies, understand how they interact with viral surface proteins, and use those insights to inform rational vaccine design. This work moves from molecular studies through animal models and into clinical evaluation of candidate vaccines and antibody therapies. The lab operates within large NIH- and Gates Foundation-funded consortia dedicated to HIV vaccine development. This research matters because neutralizing antibodies are considered the best predictor of vaccine-induced protection against viruses like HIV and influenza, which continue to lack effective vaccines.
Sergio Catz, PhD: The Catz lab studies intracellular vesicular transport, the system cells use to move materials internally, which underlies processes like autophagy, exocytosis, cytokine secretion, and immune cell functions such as phagocytosis and neutrophil extracellular trap formation. They focus especially on Rab GTPase proteins, which organize cell membranes during this transport, using super-resolution microscopy and functional assays, along with animal and cellular models, to study how these mechanisms work and go wrong in disease. The lab has developed high-throughput screening methods to identify small molecules that block or activate vesicular trafficking, with potential applications in coronary artery disease, lysosomal storage disorders, viral encephalitis, and autoimmune conditions like lupus. Their goal is to translate this basic cell biology into new targeted therapies.
Sumit Chanda, PhD: The Chanda lab studies how RNA viruses that pose pandemic risks interact with the immune system, using systems-based approaches and modern technologies to investigate the virus-host interface and innate immunity. Their basic research findings feed into drug discovery efforts through Calibr, Scripps Research's translational arm, aimed at developing next-generation antivirals, vaccine adjuvants, and immunotherapies. The lab has worked on viruses including influenza, Dengue, and SARS-CoV-2, and its funding comes from major sources like the Gates Foundation, the Department of Defense, and NIH programs focused on pandemic preparedness. The group also helped build Metascape, a widely used web tool for analyzing gene lists. This work matters because it links fundamental immunology to real-world antiviral drugs and vaccines, better preparing for future infectious disease outbreaks.
Michael G. Constantinides, PhD: The Constantinides Lab studies innate lymphocytes—immune cells that act as first responders at barrier tissues like the skin and digestive tract lining. The lab's central question is how the trillions of microbes living on and in us (the microbiota) shape the development and function of these immune cells, and in turn how the immune cells help regulate which microbes are present. Using this two-way dialogue between microbiota and host as a starting point, the lab is developing targeted approaches to intentionally modulate these interactions, with the goal of creating new therapies for infectious disease, autoimmune conditions, and cancer. The lab has also shown that certain gut bacteria are essential for building immune defenses during infancy. Beyond the science, the Constantinides Lab is known for strong mentorship and outreach to students from underrepresented backgrounds in STEM.
Candice Contet, PhD: The Contet Lab studies why alcohol drinking becomes excessive and how the brain adapts to chronic alcohol exposure. One line of work examines specific potassium channels (GIRK and BK) that alcohol activates directly, testing how much they contribute to intoxication, tolerance, and drinking behavior. A second line studies brain circuits involving the neuropeptide CRF and a region called the parasubthalamic nucleus, looking at how these systems drive the transition to alcohol dependence. The lab also runs exploratory projects using untargeted proteomics and network analysis to find new molecular drivers of heavy drinking. Methods include genetically engineered mouse models, viral vectors, and collaborations bringing in electrophysiology, mass spectrometry, and bioinformatics. The ultimate goal is identifying vulnerable populations and developing better treatments for alcohol use disorder.
Benjamin Cravatt, PhD: The Cravatt Lab develops chemistry-based tools to understand what proteins actually do inside cells and to turn that understanding into new drugs. Their signature technology, activity-based protein profiling (ABPP), measures whether an enzyme is actively working—not just how much of it is present—since activity, not abundance, usually determines a protein's real role in health and disease. ABPP profiles act like molecular fingerprints of cells and tissues, revealing new disease markers and, importantly, can also be used to discover small-molecule drug candidates that bind these proteins directly in living systems. The lab pairs this technology development with deep studies of specific proteins relevant to the nervous system and cancer, such as the enzymes FAAH and MAGL involved in the endocannabinoid system, using chemical, biochemical, genetic, and pharmacological approaches together.
Juan C. De La Torre, PhD: The De La Torre Lab studies mammarenaviruses—enveloped viruses with a two-part RNA genome that include lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV), a key model for studying virus-host interactions, as well as Lassa and Junin viruses, which cause severe hemorrhagic fevers in humans. The lab pioneered 'reverse genetics' systems that let researchers rebuild these viruses from cloned DNA, engineer specific mutations, and then observe how those changes affect infection. This approach has enabled them to identify how these viruses interact with host cell proteins and to find molecules that block those interactions, forming the basis for new antiviral drugs. The lab has also engineered weakened (attenuated) versions of LCMV and Lassa virus that fully protect animals from lethal infection after a single dose, laying groundwork for live-attenuated vaccines against these pathogens.
Ashok Deniz, PhD: The Deniz Lab studies the basic physics governing proteins, RNA, and other biological molecules, and builds new single-molecule tools to observe them directly. A major focus is Intrinsically Disordered Proteins (IDPs)—proteins that lack a fixed 3D shape and instead have flexible, shifting structures. Using single-molecule methods, the lab has shown how tunable these IDP structures are, with direct relevance to diseases like Parkinson's and Alzheimer's. The lab also studies 'condensates' or membraneless organelles—dynamic droplet-like assemblies formed by proteins, RNA, and other molecules (examples include the nucleolus and stress granules)—examining their liquid-like, viscoelastic, or solid material properties and how these properties affect cell function. Their single-molecule fluorescence methods more broadly let researchers directly test biological models of molecular structure and dynamics rather than relying on indirect measurements.
Christian Diercks, PhD: The Diercks Lab uses a system they call T7-ORACLE, which drives continuous rapid mutation and evolution in E. coli, to evolve proteins for medical and biotechnology applications faster than conventional lab evolution allows. Current projects include repurposing the botulinum toxin (Botox) protease as a potential cancer and pain therapeutic, evolving enzyme replacement therapies for lysosomal storage diseases, improving the specificity of antibodies through affinity maturation, and developing new methods to expand the genetic code. The lab is also extending directed evolution beyond biological molecules to engineered, non-biological nanomaterials—for example, evolving nanostructured materials to better deliver genes into specific tissues and cells, escape from cellular compartments, and traffic properly once inside cells. The lab's approach targets problems considered too slow or labor-intensive for standard evolution techniques in academic settings.
Ilia Droujinine, PhD: The Droujinine Lab studies how organs communicate with each other and with other individuals through secreted proteins—a signaling network that is still poorly mapped despite its central role in conditions like obesity and diabetes. The lab built a method called BirA*G3 that tracks secreted protein trafficking between organs in living Drosophila (fruit flies), which led to identifying a fat-body-derived protein that regulates muscle activity through a specific receptor. They have since developed mice carrying the same BirA*G3 system to identify secreted proteins and peptides that are altered by physiological changes or disease, and to work out their functions and mechanisms. The lab also studies how secreted proteins from other individuals can influence behavior. The long-term goal is understanding how this interorgan communication breaks down in metabolic disease and aging, to inform new therapeutics.
Cindy Ehlers, PhD: The Ehlers Lab studies genetic risk and protective factors for alcoholism, with particular focus on Native American, African American, and Hispanic American populations. The lab examines natural variation in genes encoding alcohol-metabolizing enzymes across ethnic groups and conducts genome-wide scans to find additional genes linked to alcoholism risk. This genetic information is combined with data on clinical course and environmental risk factors to describe how substance dependence develops and to design prevention and intervention programs tailored to different ethnic groups. A second research focus examines the toxic effects of alcohol on the developing fetal and adolescent brain. The lab's broader work also connects biology, culture, and trauma to mental health outcomes, informing culturally grounded prevention programs.
Sandra Encalada, PhD: The Encalada Lab studies how cells transport essential cargo along axons—the long, narrow fibers neurons use to send signals to each other—and what happens when that transport system breaks down. When cargo transport fails, it can create molecular 'traffic jams' inside neurons that lead to the buildup of toxic protein clumps, a process linked to neurodegenerative diseases including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Huntington's, and prion disorders. The lab investigates the cellular pathways underlying this toxic aggregate formation and is working to identify therapeutic agents that could stop or even reverse the process. Their findings on how these traffic jams and toxic aggregates form are informing new approaches to treating neurodegeneration more broadly, beyond any single disease.
Keary Engle, PhD: The Engle Lab focuses on catalysis-based chemistry to make small organic molecules—the building blocks of most medicines, biological research probes, agrochemicals, and industrial materials—easier and cleaner to produce. Conventional methods for making these molecules often require many synthetic steps, generate significant chemical waste, and demand extensive troubleshooting. The lab develops new catalytic reactions aimed at making chemical synthesis more efficient, effective, and environmentally sustainable, directly supporting greener approaches to drug development and manufacturing. Because these projects sit at the intersection of synthetic organic, physical organic, and organometallic chemistry, students in the lab also gain training in related disciplines beyond core chemistry. The lab's work has been recognized with awards for advancing green chemistry principles in real-world drug and materials production.
Michael Erb, PhD: The Erb Lab develops 'proximity' drugs—molecules that work by recruiting a cell's own machinery to eliminate disease-causing proteins, including ones that cannot be targeted by conventional drugs. This approach has particular relevance to breast, prostate, and blood cancers, where the lab aims to rewire essential cellular pathways and make previously 'undruggable' proteins treatable targets. The lab has also helped show how such protein-eliminating drugs can be discovered systematically, rather than by chance, and has studied how small molecules interact with the cancer-related protein FOXA1, identifying a key binding site on its surface. Separately, the lab identified a molecule called galectin-3 as a key player in how placental cells fuse together during early pregnancy, a process that when disrupted is linked to complications like preeclampsia and restricted fetal growth.
Stefano Forli, PhD: The Forli Lab uses computer-based methods to help design new medicines. Rather than testing molecules only in a wet lab, the team builds computational models of proteins and other biological molecules to find "druggable" pockets where a drug could bind and change how the protein works. They use techniques like molecular dynamics simulations, homology modeling, and molecular docking to predict how small molecules interact with these targets, then screen large virtual libraries of compounds (high-throughput virtual screening) or design custom compound libraries to find promising drug candidates. The lab also builds and freely distributes AutoDock, a widely used software suite for docking small molecules and peptides against proteins and nucleic acids. This combination of tool-building and drug discovery aims to speed the path from basic biology to new therapies.
Martin Friedlander, MD, PhD: The Friedlander Lab studies eye diseases that damage the retina, focusing especially on a condition called macular telangiectasia (MacTel), which causes vision loss. The lab's work identified gene mutations that stop MacTel patients from making enough of an amino acid the eye needs, helping explain why the disease develops. Building on this, the group and collaborators helped develop and test a cell-based therapy (ENCELTO) in a Phase 3 clinical trial, supporting its FDA approval as the first cell-based treatment for MacTel. The lab has also studied stem cells as a way to protect or restore vision, and found that restoring a naturally occurring compound called erucamide in the eye stabilized retinal tissue in preclinical models of retinal degeneration. Together, this research spans discovering disease causes to developing and testing new treatments for blinding retinal conditions.
John Griffin, PhD: The Griffin Lab studies the biology of blood-clotting proteins and how they protect cells beyond their classic role in coagulation. Their published research shows that activated protein C, a natural blood protein, can prevent programmed cell death (apoptosis) in the cells lining blood vessels, acting through specific cell-surface receptors. This cell-protective, anti-inflammatory activity has led the lab toward new applications: a drug candidate developed over the last decade, originally aimed at easing inflammation and protecting blood vessels, is now also being explored as a potential treatment for Alzheimer's disease by protecting brain cells from damage. The lab's broader work has also pointed to potential new approaches for treating cardiovascular disease. Overall, the group works at the intersection of blood biology, inflammation, and neuroprotection to find new therapeutic strategies for vascular and neurodegenerative conditions.
Danielle Grotjahn, PhD: The Grotjahn Lab studies mitochondria, the cell's energy-producing organelles, which the lab has shown also act as sensors of cellular stress. Using advanced imaging tools -- particularly cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET) and super-resolution fluorescence microscopy -- the team visualizes mitochondria in unprecedented detail inside intact cells, connecting their molecular structure to their function. Their work has revealed how mitochondria change shape in response to genetic and environmental stress, how ribosomes attached to mitochondria alter the local membrane environment for protein import, and a new way to measure membrane thickness directly inside cells. They have also studied how DNA, magnesium, and polyphosphate interact to organize genetic material. This research aims to uncover fundamental mechanisms of mitochondrial adaptation that could inform new therapies for diseases where mitochondria are disrupted, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and cancer.
Howard Hang, PhD: The Hang Lab studies how chemical signals from microbes -- especially gut bacteria -- communicate with human cells to shape immunity and health. Many of these signaling molecules, called metabolites, come from the body's own metabolism or from diet, the microbiome, and medications, and have been hard to study mechanistically. To understand them, the lab develops chemical methods to characterize how metabolites interact with proteins, and uses animal models to discover protective factors made by specific gut bacteria species and figure out how they work. This approach has revealed new functions for metabolites in immunity and in microbial disease-causing mechanisms, as well as new protective factors from the microbiome. One finding: disabling a single bacterial protein can restore the antibiotic vancomycin's power against resistant bacteria. The lab's discoveries are generating new therapeutic leads and biomarkers for infection, inflammation, and immunotherapy.
Mia L. Huang, PhD: The Huang Lab studies glycans -- complex sugar molecules that coat the surface of cells and act as signals directing important biological processes like tissue communication, growth, and immune activation. Because glycans are structurally complex, they have historically been difficult to study, so the lab develops chemical tools to decode their function. The team combines synthetic chemistry, mass spectrometry, and protein engineering to investigate how glycans influence stem cell differentiation, musculoskeletal biology, and cancer. In one line of research, the lab identified a molecule called galectin-3 that binds sugar molecules on cell-surface proteins and helps hold placental cells together as they fuse during early pregnancy -- a process that, when it fails, can lead to complications like preeclampsia. This work is helping guide new ways to diagnose or treat conditions such as cancer, liver disease, and pregnancy complications.
Darrell Irvine, PhD: The Irvine Lab engineers new ways to direct the immune system against disease, combining principles from immunology with biotechnology and materials chemistry. The lab designs synthetic materials -- including nanotechnology and "smart" biomaterials -- to make vaccines more effective and to strengthen the immune system's attack on tumors. A major focus is vaccine development for HIV and for cancer immunotherapy: the team has designed DNA scaffolds that carry HIV vaccine proteins into the body to sharpen the immune response, and has tested vaccine regimens in non-human primates that generated antibodies capable of neutralizing multiple HIV strains, a first for the field. Beyond HIV, the lab's engineering approaches are applied broadly to infectious disease, cancer, and autoimmune conditions, aiming to translate fundamental immunology and materials science into practical vaccines and immunotherapies for hard-to-treat diseases.
Kim Janda, PhD: The Janda Lab develops vaccines and antibody-based treatments to counter opioid and synthetic drug overdoses. The team has created a vaccine that trains the immune system to rapidly neutralize fentanyl and newer synthetic fentanyl analogs, and an early proof-of-concept vaccine aimed at treating overdose from xylazine, an animal sedative increasingly mixed into street drugs. They have also developed a biologic (antibody-based treatment) that works against carfentanil, an extremely potent synthetic opioid, and shown in preclinical studies that a human antibody targeting carfentanil and fentanyl can reverse overdose effects. In related work, the lab modified an opioid-like molecule to reduce respiratory depression -- the main cause of opioid overdose deaths -- while keeping its pain-blocking effects. This vaccine- and antibody-based approach to blocking drugs before they reach the brain represents a new strategy for reducing overdose deaths.
Xin Jin, PhD: The Jin Lab studies the brain using neuroscience and genomics, with a focus on how genes shape brain development. Jin's research maps the genes and cell types involved in brain development, work recognized by a McKnight Scholar Award and a 2024 Pew Scholar award. The lab has also received major funding to study interoception, the body's ability to sense its own internal state -- sometimes described as a "sixth sense" -- as part of a $14.2 million effort to map this system in humans. Separately, the lab is investigating how environmental pollution may contribute to autism risk and how specific genes raise the risk of psychiatric disorders. Together, this work aims to connect genetics, brain circuitry, and environmental factors to better understand both healthy brain development and the origins of neurodevelopmental and psychiatric conditions.
Jeffery Kelly, PhD: The Kelly lab studies how proteins fold correctly, and what goes wrong when they misfold or clump together into aggregates, causing diseases like Alzheimer's and amyloid disorders (including heart and nerve disease from transthyretin and light-chain amyloid). Using chemistry, biophysics, and cell biology, the lab designs small molecules that stabilize proteins or block harmful aggregation; this work led to the FDA-approved drug tafamidis, which slows a fatal heart and nerve disease. The lab also runs cell-based screens to find drugs that boost the cell's natural protein-quality-control systems, studies how sugar modifications can stabilize proteins, and is developing chaperone molecules to fix misfolded enzymes in lysosomal storage diseases. Their broader goal is discovering new therapeutic strategies for degenerative diseases rooted in protein misfolding, combining synthetic chemistry with biological collaboration across labs.
Megan Ken, MD, PhD: The Ken lab combines computational modeling with experiments to understand how RNA molecules fold, move, and interact with proteins, especially in viruses. They use molecular dynamics simulations and docking tools (like AutoDock) to predict RNA structures and screen small molecules that could bind and disrupt RNA function, with a focus on HIV. A major project models how HIV's genomic RNA interacts with the viral Gag protein, a process essential for packaging new virus particles; the lab uses high-throughput mutation experiments to measure how thousands of RNA changes affect this interaction in test tubes and in cells. The goal is to build accurate, quantitative models of RNA-protein interactions that reveal fundamental biology and guide the design of new RNA-targeting antiviral drugs.
Ann Kennedy, PhD: The Kennedy lab studies how the brain enables learning, decision-making, and goal-directed behavior. They investigate how populations of neurons in specific brain regions represent information: the hypothalamus (social and defensive behavior), the basal ganglia (behavior selection), and the hippocampus (social bonding). Using tools from dynamical systems theory, statistical modeling, and machine learning, the lab analyzes patterns of neural activity to understand the principles behind flexible, adaptive behavior. Their broader aim is to explain the neural basis of fundamental behaviors tied to fear, survival, and social interaction, and to understand what breaks down in conditions involving social dysfunction or excessive fear and anxiety. This work bridges computational modeling and experimental neuroscience to connect brain activity patterns to real-world behavior.
Dorothee Kern, PhD: The Kern lab studies how proteins move, not just their static 3D shapes, arguing that this constant motion ('the dance of proteins') is essential to understanding both healthy function and disease. They combine experimental techniques like NMR spectroscopy, x-ray crystallography, cryo-EM, and fluorescence spectroscopy with computational methods including molecular dynamics simulations and AI, to create atomic-resolution 'protein movies' showing how enzymes, signaling proteins, and drug targets shift between different shapes over time. This dynamic view has revealed how protein motion controls enzyme activity, cell signaling, and immune cell maturation. A major application is drug design: by exploiting differences in dynamics between a drug target and similar proteins, the lab develops more selective drugs with fewer side effects, work that has already been translated into biotech companies developing new therapeutics.
Luke Lairson, PhD: The Lairson lab, based in Scripps Research's chemistry department, studies multiple sclerosis (MS), an autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks myelin, the protective coating around neurons in the central nervous system, causing muscle weakness, cognitive problems, and progressive loss of function. Rather than only suppressing the immune attack, Lairson's research focuses on the body's own repair mechanisms, specifically the pathways that activate endogenous stem cells to regenerate lost myelin. The goal is to develop new therapies that work alongside existing MS treatments to halt disease progression by promoting natural repair rather than just symptom management. This repair-focused approach targets an unmet need in MS treatment, since current therapies do not fully reverse the damage already done to the nervous system.
Katja Lamia, PhD: The Lamia lab studies circadian rhythms, the roughly 24-hour internal clocks that let the body coordinate physiology with the daily light-dark cycle, and what happens when these rhythms are disrupted. Their research connects circadian disruption (such as from long-term shift work) to metabolic disorders, weight control problems, and increased cancer risk, and has identified a family of temperature-responsive genes implicated in cancer. The lab's work is reshaping understanding of how metabolism is regulated, pointing toward new drug strategies for metabolic disease. They also collaborate with other Scripps Research and Salk Institute scientists on related cancer therapeutics. Overall, the lab combines circadian biology with metabolism and cancer research to explain how disruptions to the body's internal clock contribute to serious disease.
Gabriel Lander, PhD: The Lander lab develops and applies cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) techniques to visualize the molecular machines inside cells at very high resolution. They improve specimen preparation, data collection, and image-processing methods to push what cryo-EM can resolve, then combine these images with biochemical and cellular experiments to study how cells maintain balance and respond to stress. A central focus is protein degradation: the large molecular machines that recognize, unfold, and destroy damaged or unneeded proteins through coordinated shape changes and motor-like motions. By linking these mechanisms to human disease and testing small molecules that can modulate protein degradation, the lab aims to open new therapeutic avenues for conditions including cancer, heart disease, and neurodegeneration.
Keren Lasker, PhD: The Lasker lab studies biomolecular condensates, membraneless compartments that cells use to organize their chemistry through a process called phase separation. Using PopZ, a disordered protein found in bacteria, as a model system, they investigate how condensates assemble, control their material properties, and select which proteins to concentrate inside them, combining cryo-electron tomography, high-resolution live-cell imaging, quantitative biophysics, and computational modeling. Building on this understanding, the lab engineers synthetic condensates in human cells that can concentrate molecular cargo, deliver it to specific locations, or capture target proteins, including disease-associated proteins that misfold or accumulate in neurodegenerative and age-related disorders. Rather than just storing captured proteins, they aim to couple this capture to the cell's own degradation machinery to promote their removal.
Amy Lightner, MD: The Lightner lab uses organoids, miniature tissue models grown from cells taken from surgical patients, to study what causes inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and to discover new treatments focused on repairing and regenerating damaged gut tissue, rather than only suppressing inflammation. These organoid models serve as a drug discovery platform both within the lab and through collaborations with other research groups. Promising treatments developed this way move into first-in-human clinical trials to test their safety and effectiveness in real patients. Dr. Lightner, a colorectal surgeon as well as a scientist, connects her clinical experience treating IBD patients directly to her lab's research goals: developing regenerative therapies that repair the intestinal lining at the root of the disease rather than just managing symptoms.
Giordano Lippi, PhD: The Lippi lab studies how neurons control where and when they produce proteins, a challenge unique to neurons because of the long distances between the cell body and its far-reaching dendrites and axon. This local control of protein production is essential for the rapid changes underlying brain plasticity and for the dramatic changes in gene expression neurons undergo as they develop and connect with the right partners. The lab focuses on microRNAs (miRNAs), small non-coding RNA molecules that fine-tune gene expression and are enriched in the brain; the lab has built new tools, including a peptide for fast reversible miRNA inhibition and mouse models for mapping miRNA-target interactions in specific neuron types. Because miRNA dysregulation is linked to disorders like autism, schizophrenia, and epilepsy, this work aims to reveal how miRNAs shape brain development and function.
Stuart A. Lipton, MD, PhD: The Lipton lab studies the molecular basis of neurodegenerative and neurodevelopmental diseases, including Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, vascular dementia, and autism-spectrum disorder. Dr. Lipton discovered protein S-nitrosylation, a chemical modification of proteins, and used this knowledge to help develop the FDA-approved Alzheimer's drug memantine, later combining it with S-nitrosylation chemistry to create NitroSynapsin, an experimental drug that protects synapses and improves behavior in animal models. His lab also discovered the MEF2C transcription factor, a master regulator of neurogenesis from brain stem cells whose disruption contributes to several of these diseases. Using human stem-cell-derived 2D cultures and 3D brain organoid models alongside techniques like patch-clamp electrophysiology and calcium imaging, the lab investigates how faulty redox and S-nitrosylation signaling damages synapses, aiming to develop new neuroprotective drugs.
Tiantian Liu: The Liu lab studies antigen-presenting cells (APCs) — immune cells that activate T cells — focusing on the gene regulatory networks that control how different APC subsets develop and specialize. Using genetically engineered mouse models, the lab investigates the distinct and overlapping roles these subsets play in shaping T cell responses. APCs are central immune regulators: they process and display signals from pathogens or tumors to T cells, helping the body distinguish threats from healthy tissue while keeping the immune system balanced. The lab's long-term goal is to translate this basic understanding of APC biology into new vaccines and immune-modulating therapies for infectious diseases, autoimmune disorders, and cancer. The PI trained as a postdoctoral associate in Kenneth Murphy's laboratory at Washington University School of Medicine before joining Scripps Research as newly appointed faculty.
Yuzhong Liu, PhD: The Liu lab combines synthetic biology, enzyme engineering, and microbial fermentation to produce and modify complex natural products — molecules originally made by plants and microbes that underlie many important medicines. A major focus is glycosides, particularly saponin-based vaccine adjuvants like QS-21, which boosts vaccine effectiveness but is traditionally harvested destructively from soapbark trees. By engineering yeast with pathway engineering and enzyme discovery/evolution, the lab has found ways to produce QS-21 and related sugar-modified molecules more sustainably. The lab also studies how sugar groups on natural products affect how molecules behave in the body and interact with the immune system, aiming to build next-generation vaccine adjuvants and cancer therapies. Ultimately, the group wants to use natural and engineered enzymes as programmable catalytic tools to synthesize new vaccines, therapeutics, and functional materials.
Martin Lotz, MD: The Lotz lab studies the molecular biology of connective tissues — cartilage and tendon — with an emphasis on aging and joint disease. Published work from the lab has examined how the transcriptional coactivator PGC-1 alpha partners with the protein Sox9 to regulate chondrogenesis, the process by which cartilage-forming cells develop, and how extracellular vesicles (small cell-released particles) contribute to cartilage homeostasis and the breakdown seen in osteoarthritis. Related Scripps Research work associated with the lab found that a mutation in the touch-sensing PIEZO1 ion channel affects tendon biology and physical performance in mice, pointing to mechanical-sensing pathways as a factor in musculoskeletal tissue function. Together, this research aims to understand what causes cartilage and tendon to age and degrade, with relevance to osteoarthritis and to broader questions about how the body ages.
Ian MacRae, PhD: The MacRae lab studies RNA interference (RNAi), a natural mechanism cells use to silence specific genes, which plays roles in antiviral defense, development, stem cell division, and memory. The lab combines structural biology, biochemistry, and cell biology to understand the molecular machinery behind RNAi — specifically the RNA-Induced Silencing Complexes (RISCs) that carry out gene silencing, and the RISC-loading complex that "programs" these complexes to target specific genetic sequences. Recent work has produced high-resolution structural images of the human protein Argonaute 2 in action, revealing why some small interfering RNA (siRNA) molecules silence genes more effectively than others, guiding the design of more effective siRNA-based therapies. The lab's broader goal is to use this mechanistic understanding of RNAi to help develop RNAi-based therapeutics for treating human disease.
Anton Maximov, PhD: The Maximov lab studies how the brain forms and stores memories, focusing on the molecular, cellular, and circuit-level mechanisms that shape neuronal connectivity in the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory, emotion, and navigation. Using genetic, biophysical, and behavioral techniques alongside optical imaging, serial electron microscopy, and computational analysis, the lab examines how networks of excitatory and inhibitory neurons are reorganized as animals learn, and how these changes contribute to encoding memories. The lab also combines human genetics data, unbiased genetic screens, and mouse models to identify the molecular basis of synaptic plasticity, and designs new small-molecule tools to manipulate specific, behaviorally relevant groups of neurons. This work aims to reveal the physical basis of memory and has implications for treating memory loss and cognitive decline linked to aging and neurodegenerative disease.
Alejandra Mendoza, PhD: The Mendoza lab studies how the nervous and immune systems communicate at "barrier tissues" — surfaces like the skin that interface with the outside environment — to sense and respond to stimuli such as temperature, injury, chemical stress, and infection. One research theme examines how sensory neurons detect and influence inflammation, including how endogenous opioid signaling mediates communication between neurons and immune cells to regulate pain, itch, and tissue homeostasis. A second theme investigates how environmental signals at barrier tissues shape immune cell activation states — effector, memory, and regulatory populations — and how their spatial organization governs protective immunity, chronic inflammation, and tissue function. By bridging neuroscience and immunology, the lab aims to understand how the body interprets environmental signals to guide immune decisions relevant to infection, tumor growth, and chronic inflammatory disease.
David Millar, PhD: The Millar lab studies the dynamic structural changes that occur during DNA processing and RNA catalysis, using time-resolved and single-molecule fluorescence techniques combined with site-directed mutagenesis. One project examines how DNA polymerases proofread their own errors, tracking how a DNA strand moves between the enzyme's polymerization site and a separate exonuclease site that corrects mistakes, underlying high-fidelity DNA replication. Another project uses fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET) to watch, in real time, how the hairpin ribozyme — a small catalytic RNA — folds and docks its substrate-binding and catalytic domains, identifying which parts stabilize the active conformation. The lab also applies single-molecule FRET to Holliday junctions, four-stranded DNA structures formed during genetic recombination and repair. This basic biophysical chemistry research aims to understand the molecular mechanisms that keep DNA replication accurate and RNA catalysis functional.
Shannon Miller, PhD: The Miller lab develops gene-editing technologies for use inside living organisms (in vivo), aiming to make genome editing a safe, practical cure for genetic disease. Genome editing currently faces obstacles including toxicity, limits on what kinds of DNA changes are possible, and difficulty delivering editing molecules to the right cells — problems the lab tackles through protein engineering, directed evolution, and both viral and non-viral delivery methods. Current work focuses on three areas: engineering improved AAV viral vectors that are easier to manufacture and deliver in vivo, developing new methods for large-scale DNA manipulations, and improving CRISPR-based therapeutics using fully chemically modified guide RNAs. Related published work includes using base editing to correct sickle cell disease in mice and engineering Cas9 variants with broader targeting capabilities — applied, translational work aimed at bringing gene-editing therapies closer to clinical use.
Marco Mravic, PhD: The Mravic lab uses protein design and computational modeling to study how proteins behave within cell membranes, an environment that is notoriously hard to study experimentally. The lab pursues three linked directions: designing small synthetic membrane proteins as simplified model systems to test basic biophysical questions about protein structure and function; creating custom chemical-biology tools that target the lipid-embedded regions of membrane proteins to probe their mechanisms and potential as drug targets; and running molecular dynamics simulations that integrate diverse experimental data to model key molecular events at membranes. Methods span computational approaches (bioinformatics, machine learning, energy calculations) and hands-on techniques including chemical protein synthesis, structural biology (X-ray, NMR, cryo-EM), cell-based assays, and biophysics. The goal is to establish general chemical "rules" governing membrane protein structure and function, relevant to disease mechanisms tied to these hard-to-study proteins.
Arthur Olson, PhD: The Olson lab develops computational and visualization tools to study how biomolecules interact — including protein-drug binding, protein-protein interactions, and the organization of molecules inside cells. The lab created AutoDock and AutoDock Vina, widely used software (with tens of thousands of users worldwide) that predicts how flexible drug-like molecules dock into protein binding sites; this supports the design of new inhibitors and chemical probes, with particular focus on anti-HIV drugs and understanding how drug resistance evolves. The lab also builds mesoscale computational models that integrate data from multiple experimental methods to represent whole cellular environments containing millions of individual molecules, and develops novel visualization approaches, including 3D printing and augmented reality, for exploring molecular structures in research and education. The FightAIDS@Home distributed-computing project, run through IBM on millions of volunteer computers, grew out of this lab's drug-discovery work.
Donghyun Raphael Park, PhD: The Park lab studies how disease-causing bacteria assemble complex molecular "nanomachines" that inject bacterial proteins into host cells and the surrounding environment, a process central to how pathogens manipulate host cell functions and cause infection. Using cryo-electron tomography (cryo-ET), a technique that images biological structures in their native, unaltered state, the lab aims to determine how these secretion nanomachines are built and how their architecture enables them to deliver bacterial substrates and drive pathogenicity. Related Scripps Research findings connected to this area include work on disabling bacterial proteins to restore antibiotic effectiveness against resistant bacteria, and on how bacterial DNA organization is maintained. By revealing the structural basis of bacterial infection machinery, the lab's research aims to open new avenues for antibacterial and phage-based therapies, especially against drug-resistant pathogens.
Christopher Parker, PhD: The Parker Lab combines organic chemistry with chemical proteomics and cell/molecular biology to study human disease at the molecular level. They design small molecules that can regulate complex biological processes, like immune responses, and use these molecules as tools to figure out which proteins go wrong in disease. One major project developed a new high-resolution method for finding potential drug targets on proteins inside living cells. The lab has also created a compound that blocks a protein long considered impossible to drug, which is involved in autoimmune diseases such as lupus, and studies metabolic and protein changes underlying aging and Alzheimer's disease. The overall goal is to turn these discoveries into chemical tools and eventually new therapeutics. This is a good fit for students interested in chemistry-driven approaches to biology and drug discovery.
Ardem Patapoutian, PhD: The Patapoutian Lab studies mechanotransduction — how cells sense physical force — which is considered the last major sense not understood at the molecular level. The lab discovered PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, ion channels that let cells detect mechanical force. Genetic studies from the lab showed PIEZO2 is essential for touch, body position sense (proprioception), and blood pressure sensing, while PIEZO1 helps control blood flow, blood pressure, and blood vessel development. They've since found other mechanosensors, including GPR68 and OSCA/TMEM63 proteins, and continue searching for new ones. Related work from the group has identified proteins that help kidney cells regulate blood pressure and has shed light on how the body detects light touch and why that process can break down in sensory disorders. Great fit for students curious about sensory biology, ion channels, and physiology.
Michael Petrascheck, PhD: The Petrascheck Lab studies aging and how it can be slowed or manipulated to prevent age-related disease. Instead of targeting diseases directly, they search for small molecules that extend lifespan, screening chemicals in the roundworm C. elegans and in mice. Small molecules are useful because they can be tested across cell lines, multiple organisms, disease models, and in combination with known aging-related mutations. The lab found that an existing antidepressant can extend lifespan in adult C. elegans, and that the antibiotic minocycline extends worm lifespan by preventing harmful protein buildup during aging. These lifespan-extending compounds are then used as research probes to understand the molecular links between aging and age-related diseases. A strong fit for students interested in aging biology, pharmacology, and model organism research.
Lisa Racki, PhD: The Racki Lab studies how bacteria survive starvation, a state they're often in during chronic infections in the human body. Most antibiotics target processes bacteria need while actively growing, like DNA replication and cell wall building, so they're less effective against starved, non-growing bacteria. The lab investigates how bacteria reorganize their internal subcellular structure to survive when nutrients run low. They discovered that long chains of molecules called polyphosphates help slow down movement inside bacterial cells, letting them enter a protective resting state — a state that helps pathogens evade antibiotics and contributes to hard-to-treat chronic infections in the lungs, blood, wounds, and on medical devices. Understanding this mechanism could point toward new ways to target slow-growing, antibiotic-evading bacteria. Good fit for students interested in microbiology and antibiotic resistance.
Chen Ran, PhD: The Ran Lab studies the body's internal senses — how the brain detects signals like hunger, fullness, thirst, nausea, low oxygen, and internal pain from organs. To study this, the lab built a novel imaging system that records the activity of thousands of individual neurons in the brainstem, the brain region that gateways signals from internal organs. They deliver stimuli mimicking stomach stretch, nutrient ingestion, organ pain, and more, then watch how different neurons respond. Past work from the lab found that internal organs are mapped out in an organized way in the brainstem, forming what they call a 'visceral homunculus.' The lab combines imaging, electrophysiology, genetics, optogenetics, and behavior experiments to understand these circuits, with potential relevance to hypertension, obesity, diabetes, eating disorders, and nausea. A strong fit for students interested in neuroscience and physiology.
Marisa Roberto, PhD: The Roberto Lab studies how alcohol and other drugs of abuse (like nicotine and cocaine) change the brain at the level of synapses, the connections between neurons. They focus especially on the central nucleus of the amygdala, a brain region central to both drug-related behavior and responses to fear and stress. Using electrophysiology, pharmacology, and molecular methods, the lab has identified specific changes in GABA and glutamate signaling caused by alcohol dependence, and found that the anti-epileptic drug gabapentin can reverse some behavioral effects of alcohol dependence, suggesting it could be repurposed as a treatment. They also study stress-related neuropeptides like corticotropin-releasing factor (CRF), nociceptin, oxytocin, and neuropeptide Y, and how these systems drive both 'reward' and 'relief' drinking. Great fit for students interested in neuroscience, addiction, and pharmacology.
Edward Roberts, PhD: Edward Roberts works in medicinal and organic chemistry, developing small-molecule drugs, with a focus on compounds that act on the sphingosine 1-phosphate (S1P) receptor. This research contributed to the discovery of ozanimod, a drug developed at Scripps Research that has received FDA and European approval for treating multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis, and is being studied for Crohn's disease. He has also studied how genetically and pharmacologically manipulating the TLR4 receptor affects ethanol consumption in rodent models, connecting immune signaling to alcohol-related behavior. His work has been recognized for contributions to organic synthesis and the development of medicinally useful compounds. A good fit for students interested in medicinal chemistry and how lab discoveries move toward real, FDA-approved drugs.
Hugh Rosen, MD, PhD: Hugh Rosen is a physician-scientist focused on turning basic biology discoveries into approved medicines, working partly through Calibr, Scripps Research's drug discovery division. He co-invented ozanimod, an approved treatment for multiple sclerosis and ulcerative colitis, and navacaprant, a drug now in Phase 3 trials that showed meaningful improvement for people with moderate-to-severe major depressive disorder by targeting a specific brain circuit. His group has also developed first-in-class molecules that block a specific protein interaction in immune cells, offering a potential targeted approach to autoimmune diseases like lupus and rheumatoid arthritis, aiming to reduce inflammation without weakening the immune system overall. A strong fit for students interested in translational medicine — the path from lab discovery to real clinical treatments.
Enrique Saez, PhD: The Saez Lab studies how the body regulates energy balance, focusing on two areas. First, they study nuclear receptors — proteins that sense dietary components like fats, vitamins, and cholesterol-related molecules and turn genes on or off in response — using high-throughput cell-based screens and animal models to find new nutrient-sensing pathways. Second, they study the genetic regulation of energy storage in fat (adipose) tissue, using genomic and chemical approaches to find genes that control fat tissue formation. Their findings include a protein normally abundant in fat tissue that, when missing, disrupts glucose and insulin regulation, and a compound that enhanced a metabolism-related enzyme and reversed signs of diabetes in mice. The goal is to find new therapeutic targets for obesity and diabetes. Good fit for students interested in metabolism and gene regulation.
Pietro Paolo Sanna, MD: Pietro Paolo Sanna's research spans drug abuse and addiction, genomics, HIV/AIDS, neurobiology, and viral diseases. His lab's work has shown, by examining RNA in hundreds of thousands of individual brain cells, that alcohol use disorder may accelerate the progression of Alzheimer's disease, and separate studies from the group found that heavy drinking can speed cognitive decline in animals genetically predisposed to Alzheimer's. The lab has also developed methods for converting skin cells into different types of neurons (described as a 'neuronal cookbook'), contributed to research using patients' own cells toward future Parkinson's disease treatments, and studied early brain development differences in patients with Fragile X syndrome. Good fit for students interested in neurobiology, addiction, and the links between substance use and neurodegenerative disease.
William Schief, PhD: The Schief Lab designs vaccines, with a major focus on HIV, using an approach called germline-targeting vaccine design that trains the immune system's earliest antibody-producing cells toward the right response. The lab works on universal vaccines meant to protect against many variants of a virus at once, with progress reported for influenza, HIV, and coronavirus. They've developed nanodisc platforms to get a clearer view of how viral proteins interact with antibodies, and used computer modeling to understand how antibodies use lipid molecules to recognize HIV. Two HIV vaccine clinical trials led in part by this lab showed proof of concept for generating broadly neutralizing antibodies, a key step toward an effective HIV vaccine. The lab also works on mRNA vaccines, nanoparticle design, and protein structure. Excellent fit for students interested in immunology and vaccine development.
Peter Schultz, PhD: The Schultz lab pioneers ways to expand the genetic code, engineering cells to incorporate unnatural amino acids that let researchers control and study proteins in new ways (for example, using a genetically encoded "photocaged" amino acid to switch protein phosphorylation on and off with light). This chemistry underpins large-scale, diversity-based approaches to discovering novel proteins, drugs, and materials, including a platform for fast, scalable protein evolution used to find new therapies, diagnostics, and predict drug-resistance mutations. The lab has also engineered enzymes, such as a reprogrammed botulinum toxin protease, to selectively break down disease-causing proteins in human cells. Applications span cancer immunotherapy, infectious disease, and regenerative medicine for damaged heart, lung, and intestinal tissue. The work sits at the interface of chemistry and biology, aiming to translate fundamental protein-engineering tools into next-generation medicines.
Ian B. Seiple, PhD: The Seiple lab combines medicinal chemistry, microbiology, and structural biology to fight drug-resistant bacterial infections. A core project develops fully synthetic routes to natural-product antibiotic scaffolds (streptogramins and lankacidins) that block bacterial protein synthesis, informed by structural binding data and known resistance pathways, including cryo-EM studies of how their antibiotic analogs act on the ribosome. Another effort re-engineers antibiotics effective only against Gram-positive bacteria so they can also kill harder-to-treat Gram-negative pathogens, exploiting bacterial periplasm enzymes. The lab also collaborates on a CRISPRi platform for high-throughput screening of microbial extracts for new antibiotics, and, separately, on antibody-based approaches to degrade cancer-causing proteins and on ultra-high-resolution expansion microscopy techniques. Overall, the group develops new chemistry-driven strategies against infectious disease and antibiotic resistance, alongside methods work in imaging and protein degradation.
K. Barry Sharpless, PhD: Sharpless is a two-time Nobel laureate in chemistry, recognized for developing "click chemistry" (shared with Carolyn Bertozzi and Morten Meldal, 2022) and for chirally catalyzed oxidation reactions (2001). Click chemistry is an approach for reliably and efficiently snapping molecular building blocks together, making it far easier to construct complex molecules for drug discovery and materials science. His group's work has included discovering new, easy, and efficient chemical reactions for building potential new drug molecules, and generating libraries of polymers through environmentally safer synthetic routes. The lab's broader contributions to synthetic organic chemistry have been recognized with major awards, including the Robert Robinson Award. In short, this is a chemistry lab focused on inventing simpler, more reliable reactions for assembling molecules used in medicine and materials.
Ryan Shenvi, PhD: The Shenvi lab works at the intersection of organic chemistry and biomedicine. On the biomedical side, they study opioid receptor ligands like salvinorin A and GB18 (derived from a traditional Papua New Guinean medicine), engineering them into selective, G protein-biased opioid agonists, alongside programs on 14-3-3 protein-client molecular glues, GABAa receptor antagonists, and SDH inhibitors. On the chemistry side, the lab is known for establishing metal hydride atom transfer (MHAT) as a mechanism enabling cheap metals like iron, manganese, and cobalt to build complex molecular bonds in new outer-sphere ways, complementing traditional palladium catalysis. They develop experimental and computational tools to better access, explore, and predict the behavior of structurally complex, information-rich molecules, then apply these tools and molecules toward biomedical goals such as new drug synthesis routes and quaternary-carbon-containing compounds.
Supriya Srinivasan, PhD: The Srinivasan lab studies the gut-brain axis as a central regulator of metabolism, investigating how the intestine and nervous system communicate through neuroendocrine and enteroendocrine signaling to control energy balance, feeding behavior, fat metabolism, and lifespan. Using C. elegans as a genetically tractable model system with well-mapped neural circuitry, the lab runs large-scale genetic and small-molecule screens to identify conserved molecular pathways involving GPCRs, neuropeptides, and insulin-like signaling that let animals sense internal physiological state and mount coordinated responses. One discovery identified a molecule from roundworm intestines that signals the brain to slow fat loss during food scarcity. The lab has extended this work into mammalian intestinal biology, studying how gut-hormone signals affect lipid mobilization, mucosal immunity, and inflammation, with relevance to obesity, type 2 diabetes, inflammatory bowel disease, and healthy aging.
Lisa Stowers Anderson, PhD: The Stowers lab studies how the brain detects and interprets chemical signals like pheromones and odors. Their work has shown that the vomeronasal organ mediates defensive behaviors between species by detecting protein pheromone homologs, and has characterized species-specific major urinary proteins and male pheromones that accelerate female reproductive organ development. More recently, the lab has worked to map a complete neural circuit in a mammalian brain, tracing how olfactory and pheromone signals are recognized and processed, and has extended this interest to interoception, the connections between the brain and internal organs like the heart and stomach. Overall, this is a neuroscience lab focused on decoding the neural circuitry underlying chemosensation, innate social/defensive behaviors, and brain-body communication.
Andrew Su, PhD: The Su lab applies computer science, statistics, and AI to biomedical discovery, with a strong commitment to open source, open data, and open science. They build computational tools and infrastructure to organize biomedical knowledge at scale, including the widely used BioThings suite (MyGene.info, MyVariant.info, MyChem.info), which together serve over 30 million API requests monthly, and contribute to large-scale knowledge graphs like the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator and NIAID Data Ecosystem that integrate data across hundreds of sources for computational querying. The lab collaborates with experimental scientists on single-cell transcriptomics, circadian biology, and infectious disease data, translating large datasets into testable hypotheses. Most recently, they are exploring agentic AI and large language models for science, building tools that help researchers generate ideas, synthesize literature, and collaborate, emphasizing transparency and reliability.
John Teijaro, PhD: The Teijaro lab studies viral infection and the immune system using mouse models of LCMV (persistent infection) and influenza (acute infection). Teijaro's research focuses on how type 1 interferon signaling drives cytokine amplification and immune pathology, and how it initiates and maintains persistent viral infection. Earlier work established that memory CD4 T cells can protect against influenza independently of CD8 T cells or B cells (via interferon-gamma), identified tissue-resident memory CD4 T cells in the lung, and showed that endothelial (not epithelial) cells drive damaging cytokine amplification during influenza, with blunting this response improving survival. The lab also found that blocking type 1 interferon signaling during persistent LCMV infection speeds viral clearance by reducing immune activation and restoring lymphoid tissue architecture. Related work has yielded first-in-class molecules targeting immune protein interactions relevant to lupus and rheumatoid arthritis.
Luc Teyton, MD, PhD: The Teyton lab pursues two main research lines. First, in response to rising antibiotic resistance, they engineer therapeutic anti-microbial antibodies by targeting glycans in bacterial and fungal cell walls, using synthetic conjugate immunogens to elicit very high-affinity antibodies; this approach has shown proof-of-concept efficacy against Streptococcus pneumoniae and antibiotic-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, guided by structural studies and synthetic chemistry, with a goal of reaching human clinical trials. Second, for over 25 years the lab has studied how immune cells destroy insulin-producing beta cells in type 1 diabetes, examining the normal relationship between the endocrine pancreas and immune system and how it breaks down, using genetics and immunology in mice and humans, including islet organoids, single-cell analysis, and clinical patient sampling, aiming to identify markers and therapeutic targets for the disease.
Eric Topol, MD: Eric Topol directs the Scripps Research Translational Institute, where his group works at the intersection of cardiology, digital health, and artificial intelligence. As a practicing cardiologist and researcher, he studies how AI and digital tools (wearables, genetic data, large datasets) can be applied to predict and manage disease and personalize medicine, work summarized in his books including Deep Medicine and Super Agers. His team runs digital clinical trials, including a current study testing whether a GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist (already approved for type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea) can relieve long COVID symptoms. Topol has published extensively on self-supervised learning in medicine and the convergence of human and artificial intelligence in healthcare, positioning the Institute as a hub for translating AI-driven insights into real-world clinical trials.
Ali Torkamani, PhD: Torkamani directs Genomics and Genome Informatics at the Scripps Research Translational Institute, using genomic and informatic technologies to understand the genetic basis of human disease and predict individual health risks. His lab's major focus areas include interpreting the human genome, discovering the genetics of novel rare diseases, and building machine- and deep-learning models that combine genetic and clinical data to predict risk for common diseases such as coronary artery disease and pre-diabetes. The lab develops app-based digital tools and wearable-sensor approaches that analyze genetic and physiological markers to forecast cardiovascular and metabolic disease risk, work that is being integrated into remote clinical trials offering personalized behavioral and therapeutic interventions. The overarching goal is to decode genetic and physiological signals well enough to predict and guide interventions that restore individuals to their personal health baseline.
Renan V.H. de Carvalho, PhD: The Laboratory of Immune Longevity studies why some immune responses last a lifetime while others fade. The lab's top priority is plasma cell longevity: what makes certain antibody-producing cells persist for years and keep producing protective antibodies, and why that durable immunity often fails to develop. The team uses transgenic mouse models combined with infection and immunization experiments to trace the biological steps that lead to long-lasting immunity. Related past work from the lab's PI has also examined how immune sensors like the NLRP3 inflammasome respond to pathogens such as Leishmania. The broader goal is understanding what separates a short-lived immune response from one that protects for decades, which matters directly for designing longer-lasting vaccines, including for diseases like HIV and respiratory viruses.
Julia Moore Vogel, PhD: This group runs participant-centered health research and clinical trials focused on complex, hard-to-study illnesses, with a particular emphasis on long COVID. Rather than requiring patients to come into a clinic, studies are decentralized: they use digital technologies, wearable sensors, and at-home biospecimen collection so people across the country and world can take part. One current project is a digital clinical trial testing whether a GIP/GLP-1 dual receptor agonist (a drug class already approved for type 2 diabetes, obesity, and sleep apnea) can ease long COVID symptoms. The lab's leader also studies and lives with long COVID herself, informing her focus on improving symptom management and health equity for affected patients. This matters because long COVID affects millions and still lacks proven treatments.
Andrew Ward, PhD: This lab studies membrane proteins and viruses using structural biology methods, aiming to see molecules in atomic-level detail. One research line investigates membrane transporters, proteins that shuttle molecules across the cell surface, using x-ray crystallography, electron microscopy, and other biophysical techniques to work out how they function. A second line focuses on viral surface proteins, like those on HIV and influenza, which viruses use to latch onto and enter human cells. The lab uses single-particle electron microscopy and electron tomography to visualize how broadly neutralizing antibodies (rare antibodies effective against many strains) bind and block these viral proteins. This structural information helps explain how such antibodies work and guides the design of better vaccine components meant to elicit similar protective antibodies in people, particularly against HIV and influenza.
Friedbert Weiss, PhD: This lab studies the neurobiology of drug and alcohol addiction, focusing on how the brain's motivation and reward circuits go wrong. Using animal models, the team investigates the neuropharmacological, neurocircuitry, and molecular mechanisms behind dependence and withdrawal, drug and alcohol craving, relapse, and the memory and cognitive impairments that come with addiction. Recent work from the lab has shown that alcohol-seeking can be driven by a need for relief from negative states, not just for pleasure, and has identified specific brain regions that both motivate and can suppress compulsive drug-seeking behavior. This research matters because it points toward more targeted treatments for alcohol use disorder and other addictions, particularly strategies aimed at reducing cravings and relapse in people recovering from substance dependence.
James Williamson, PhD: This lab studies how RNA molecules fold into 3D shapes and interact with proteins to carry out their biological roles. A major focus is ribosome assembly: using techniques like isotope pulse-chase mass spectrometry, single-molecule fluorescence, and time-resolved electron microscopy (in collaboration with other labs), the team tracks how ribosomal proteins bind together over time, both in test tubes and inside living cells. Other projects use x-ray crystallography to determine the structures of RNA-protein complexes that control stem cell development in the roundworm C. elegans, regulate T-cell activation, and enable HIV replication by helping move viral RNA out of the cell nucleus. Understanding these RNA structures and assembly processes matters because it reveals fundamental mechanisms of gene expression and offers potential targets for treating diseases like HIV.
Ian Wilson, PhD: This lab uses high-resolution x-ray crystallography to determine the 3D structures of immune system molecules and the pathogens they fight, aiming to understand how the immune system recognizes and neutralizes threats. The team has solved over 250 structures of antibody fragments bound to targets ranging from small molecules to viral proteins, along with structures of T-cell receptors, MHC molecules, and innate immune sensors like Toll-like receptors. A major focus is HIV-1 and influenza: the lab has mapped nearly all known broadly neutralizing antibodies against HIV's envelope proteins and discovered shared vulnerable sites on influenza's surface proteins, including insights from the historically devastating 1918 flu virus. This structural work directly informs vaccine design, showing scientists which viral sites to target so that vaccines can trigger broadly protective antibody responses.
R. Luke Wiseman, PhD: This lab studies how cells sense and respond to stress, whether from genetic changes, environmental exposure, or aging, and how failures in that response contribute to disease. The main focus is proteostasis, the cell's system for keeping proteins properly folded and functional, including three specific stress pathways: the unfolded protein response, the integrated stress response, and the heat shock response. When these pathways become imbalanced, misfolded proteins can build up and damage cells, a process implicated in neurodegenerative diseases, metabolic disorders, cardiovascular disease, and inflammatory conditions. The lab's goal is to find ways to therapeutically fine-tune these stress pathways, essentially redirecting the body's own defense systems, to correct these imbalances. The long-term aim is a 'one-drug, multiple-disease' approach that could treat several stress-related conditions through a shared mechanism.
Chi-Huey Wong, PhD: The Wong lab works at the intersection of chemistry and biology, studying glycosylation: the process by which sugar molecules attach to proteins and change how they behave. The team develops chemical and enzymatic methods to build complex sugar chains, glycoproteins, and glycan microarrays in order to study how glycosylation influences cancer progression, bacterial and viral infections, neurodegenerative disease, and immune responses. Using these tools, the lab engineers antibodies with modified sugar attachments to improve their effectiveness, designs low-sugar vaccine candidates against cancer and microbial infections, and searches for enzyme inhibitors that block disease-related sugar pathways. The lab is also building large biological datasets to support AI-driven drug discovery. This work matters because glycosylation shapes how proteins function in the body, making it a promising but underexplored target for new medicines.
Peter Wright, PhD: This lab uses nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, along with other biophysical and biochemical methods, to study how proteins are structured, how they move, and how they fold. NMR is uniquely able to capture proteins in solution and reveal the constant small structural shifts that let them function. One major focus is intrinsically disordered proteins, which lack a fixed shape but are essential to cell signaling; the lab studies transcription regulators like CBP/p300 and the tumor suppressor p53 to see how these flexible proteins fold only once they bind their targets. A second focus is protein misfolding, including how the protein transthyretin unfolds and clumps together to form amyloid, a process linked to amyloid disease. This work helps explain, at a molecular level, how proteins malfunction in disease.
Chunlei Wu, PhD: This lab builds computational tools and databases that organize biomedical and genomic information so researchers can find and use it more easily. Past work includes BioGPS and MyGene.info, gene-centric platforms for organizing online genomic data. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the lab helped build Outbreak.info, a public platform tracking the prevalence of new SARS-CoV-2 variants and bringing together pandemic research data with improved visualization, and contributed to monitoring efforts around emerging variants of concern. The lab has also worked on the Biomedical Data Translator, an open-source system funded by NIH to help researchers securely share and connect health data, and on data infrastructure projects for infectious disease research more broadly. This work matters because usable, well-organized data is a bottleneck for turning raw genomic and clinical information into scientific and medical insight.
